analysis.one_liner: Raises the cap on small-company securities offerings the SEC can exempt from registration to $50 million.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: after two hearings, it sat in the Senate Banking Committee until the Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the SEC to create an exemption from full securities registration for companies selling up to $50 million of stock or debt to the public each year, up from the $5 million cap under the existing Regulation A exemption. It directed the SEC to keep some protections — annual audited financial statements, anti-fraud liability, bad-actor disqualification rules, and optional disclosure requirements — and to review the $50 million limit every two years. It also preempts some state review of these offerings and orders a study of how state securities laws affect small offerings. The Senate Banking Committee held two hearings but never voted on the bill, so it died when the 112th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Small and mid-sized companies that want to sell stock or bonds to the public would gain a cheaper, lighter route: instead of the costly full SEC registration process, they could sell up to $50 million per year under a simplified exemption that requires audited annual financials but skips much of the standard offering paperwork. Growing companies in the gap between private placement and full public listing benefit most — existing law capped this kind of simplified offering at $5 million. Investors gain access to a new pool of small-company securities, and the wider public may see some benefit if these companies use the cheaper capital to grow and hire.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Small growing companies seeking public capital

how_it_helps.text: It raises the ceiling on securities the SEC may exempt from registration to $50 million, with the securities freely tradable and able to be sold publicly rather than restricted.

It keeps real safeguards: anti-fraud liability applies to anyone selling the securities, issuers must file audited financial statements annually, the SEC can require offering statements and periodic disclosures, and bad actors can be disqualified under standards similar to Dodd-Frank's.

It directs the SEC to review the $50 million cap every two years and report to Congress if it decides not to increase it, and orders a GAO study of how state Blue Sky laws affect smaller public offerings.

analysis.who_pays: Investors in these offerings would bear the main cost: securities sold under the exemption would not go through the full disclosure regime of a registered public offering, so buyers would have less standardized information before putting money in, and some state securities regulators would lose review authority over offerings sold on national exchanges or to qualified purchasers. The bill tries to offset this by requiring audited financial statements, keeping anti-fraud liability in place, and letting the SEC demand additional disclosures.

drawbacks.text: The bill preempts state securities regulators (Blue Sky laws) from reviewing offerings under the new exemption when sold on a national exchange or to qualified purchasers, removing one layer of state-level investor oversight.

Most investor protections — offering statements, periodic disclosures, pre-filing solicitation rules — are left to the SEC's discretion rather than required in the statute, so the actual protection investors receive depends entirely on later rulemaking.

Companies selling up to $50 million of securities publicly would do so without the full registration and disclosure regime that applies to larger public offerings, increasing the information gap facing retail investors in those deals.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside is real but modest: a lighter, cheaper path to public capital for companies too big for private offering exemptions but too small for full registration, which is exactly the tier many small issuers say is hardest to reach. The cost is a smaller federal disclosure footprint for offerings up to $50 million — public investors in those offerings would get less standardized information than registered offerings provide, relying on the SEC to impose the right conditions. The bill keeps several genuine protections in place (anti-fraud liability, audited financials, a biennial review of the cap with a required explanation if the SEC declines to raise it), which makes it better designed than a blanket deregulation. On balance a reasonable, narrow change whose main cost is reduced transparency at the margin.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced, got bipartisan support and two Banking Committee hearings, but the committee never voted on it, so it expired when the Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Senator Jon Tester introduced S. 1544 with Senator Pat Toomey on September 12, 2011; the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee.
The committee held hearings on the bill in December 2011 and March 2012 but never ordered it reported or voted on it.
The bill died in committee when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013, having never reached the Senate floor.

The bill would have amended the Securities Act of 1933 to require the SEC to create an exemption for offerings up to $50 million per year, with annual audited financial statements, issuer disqualification rules, and covered-security treatment on national exchanges.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Small companies that would have used the exemption, along with the lawyers and intermediaries who would have worked those deals, are worse off than if it passed; state regulators' authority over these offerings remained intact, which is the main thing anyone gained.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: State regulators' authority; status quo for issuers

for.name: Sen. Jon Tester
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and got it referred to the Banking Committee.

for.name: Sen. Pat Toomey
for.what_they_did: Joined as the original Republican cosponsor.

for.name: 7 cosponsors (4 Democrats, 3 Republicans)
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, giving the bill bipartisan backing.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Held hearings on the bill in December 2011 and March 2012 but never ordered it reported or brought it to a vote, letting it die in committee.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by a Democrat and cosponsored by a Republican, with a 4-3 split among its other cosponsors, so support was genuinely bipartisan; its death in committee had no recorded partisan vote.

industries.note: They would gain a cheaper path to raise up to $50 million from the public without full SEC registration, with mandatory audited financials and anti-fraud liability still applying. This is the bill's core beneficiary.

Offerings under the new exemption would be treated as federally covered securities when sold on a national exchange or to qualified purchasers, stripping state regulators of review authority over those deals.

industries.industry: Securities lawyers, underwriters, and disclosure-service firms
industries.note: A new class of public offerings would create work structuring and documenting exempted deals, while companies that previously had to pay for full registration could now avoid it. The result is a shift in who gets paid for the paperwork.

They would rely on SEC-set offering statements and periodic disclosures rather than the full registration regime, trading some transparency for broader access to these investments and cheaper capital formation.
